Review of three externally flagged artifacts, 2026-10-20

Verdicts are artifact judgements, not assertions of authorized deployment.
All three are BENIGN on the available evidence and should take the queue's
sighted-quarantine route. No malicious execution chain was recovered. Preserve
networking, cryptography, process execution, registry, and mining observations.
A clean scan and vendor metadata were not used to establish these verdicts.

4bf1306dd66f14ed59de23ede30c371e1f0900bb7053ba5b1412921e00be155d
Identification: Windows 7 DismHost 6.1.7600.16385 plus concatenated vendor PEs.
Verdict: BENIGN; original executable code, no overlay activation recovered.

The first 96,767 bytes equal the corresponding prefix of Microsoft's 96,768
byte DismHost.exe from:
https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols/dismhost.exe/4A5BC39032000/dismhost.exe
The missing final byte is padding; another MZ begins at that position. The
mapped PE sections end at 0x17a00 and the original entry point is RVA 0xf3cc.
Rizin tracing follows security-cookie initialization at 0x10000fcc0, CRT
startup at 0x10000f0b8, WinMain at 0x100007b54, COM security setup and DismHost's
command-line-controlled servicing/session logic. File mapping at
0x10000db74 opens its argument path and maps resource/module data; it does not
extract or activate the concatenated images. The primary mapped bytes have no
patch relative to Microsoft's executable. No extra TLS callback or mapped
section introduces appended code.

The appended PEs are:
  0x0179ff Oracle Java 7 U45 policytool
  0x01b7a6 UPX 3.91 executable packer (itself UPX-packed)
  0x065fa5 Microsoft Office Click-to-Run perfboost (PDB attribution)
  0x0b5c6c Adobe LogTransport2
  0x107503 Mozilla Firefox plugin-hang-ui
  0x1315aa Microsoft App-V mavinject32
  0x18b2d1 Adobe WCChromeNativeMessagingHost
  0x1bcc70 Microsoft Office icons resource-only image, entry point zero
  0x253117 Adobe AcroTextExtractor
  0x2628ae Microsoft SetupHost
  0x33aa2d Microsoft MigHost

Each intermediate appended PE is missing its final byte. On analytical copies,
restoring that padding byte permits Authenticode parsing. For all ten signed
appended images, osslsigncode's calculated image digest equals the signed
indirect-data digest. Additional DER parsing and cryptography RSA verification
confirmed the primary signer's signature over authenticated attributes and the
encapsulated-content message digest. This establishes signature integrity,
not current certificate-chain trust; expired certificates and local trust-store
failures are not silently ignored or described as trusted signing.
The last MigHost image needs no repair. The outer file has no Authenticode
signature record and an invalid checksum: embedded certificates do not sign it.

The UPX bytes also exactly equal the official upx391w/upx.exe release minus
its final padding byte, downloaded from:
https://github.com/upx/upx/releases/download/v3.91/upx391w.zip
A repaired analytical copy unpacks normally to the UPX command-line tool;
there is no basis for treating its decompression stub as a ransomware payload.
All appended content was extracted/inspected, including imports, resources,
version metadata, and the otherwise unbranded perfboost executable. Certificate
revocation URLs and Adobe telemetry strings belong to the embedded vendors.
They do not show outbound activity from the outer DismHost process.

Why the hostile source label: the supplied Triage report's static score 10 is
from a custom UPX/OEP signature plus unsigned-PE metadata. Its two dynamic
runs have score 1; the inspected behavioral run has no signatures and the
sample process exits promptly. That is corroboration, not the verdict basis.
The unexecutable collection of vendor PEs exposes packer/injection/crypto
strings to classifiers, which plausibly explains the mixed family labels.
https://tria.ge/261020-r8kx4sa14w
An unexplained concatenation is unusual. Its creator, intended external
extractor, and deployment provenance are missing; benign code does not establish
benign packaging intent. No unsupported downloader/injection claim is added.

f11834e37011385acbe45cbd9c00cf0a60577ed9a8fc0f751941aec6821d5e81
Identification: Atom's Connections 1.7.1 beta, unsigned .NET desktop host.
Verdict: BENIGN; implemented encrypted peer messaging, no hidden hostile chain.

Decoded all 17 CIL methods using dnfile/dncil, resolving member and user-string
tokens, and traced Main -> Run, argument parsing, LoadFiles, Handle, SafeTarget,
Listen, EndOtherCopies, browser opening, URL registration and shortcut creation.
Run binds HttpListener to 127.0.0.1/localhost on port 47800 (CLI configurable).
It generates a random 32-byte device key, stores it under LocalAppData using
current-user DPAPI, and retrieves only that application-owned key. It does not
collect browser passwords or unrelated DPAPI blobs. EndOtherCopies queries
Win32_Process for its own image basename and matching application port before
killing a stale instance. UseShellExecute opens the local browser URL.
Registry writes install the atoms: URL protocol under HKCU; they are not a Run
key or scheduled persistence mechanism. A .lnk is placed on the desktop.

The 254,679-byte app.pak resource is GZip data, not a native encrypted payload.
Its SHA256 equals the exact hash checked by LoadFiles:
db2fd6b4dc620bdddf8cad94e451514066e9cd8181f40ba9a4905159800ccc3c
Its unpacked members are index.html, player.html and vendor/peerjs.min.js.
The binary merely serves them as static resources. No Assembly.Load, RunPE,
resource-to-process injection, or downloaded executable launch is present.

Recovered the rotated, Base64-like JavaScript string table and 1,140 arithmetic
lookup wrappers using only isolated decoder functions in a bounded QuickJS
context; replaced 10,979 constant calls and inspected the resulting application.
The code provides AES-GCM storage/message protection, ECDH P-256 contact keys,
PBKDF2/HKDF key derivation, IndexedDB storage, invite/consent flows, PeerJS/WebRTC
messaging and user-triggered media/file exchange. Plugin HTML is placed in a
sandboxed frame with restrictive CSP and explicit application permissions.
The native /save endpoint accepts POST with an application header, rejects
cross-site requests, and confines normalized, validated relative names to its
Pictures/Documents application roots. /device-key has corresponding request
checks. This is app key delivery to its own frontend, not secret exfiltration.

The bundled PeerJS dependency is byte-identical to:
https://unpkg.com/peerjs@1.5.4/dist/peerjs.min.js
Its configured broker is 0.peerjs.com:443; default STUN/TURN facilities belong
to that library. The update path fetches version.json and offers a user-clicked
download restricted to the application's HTTPS origin; it does not execute it.
Fetched and inspected https://atomsconnections.com/, version.json, and the
linked current portable distribution. The site describes the same product.
The current published executable is a newer version, so it is supporting
context, not an asserted hash match for this older sample.

Why collected/flagged: an unsigned, high-entropy managed executable with a large
compressed resource, obfuscated JavaScript, WMI process termination, DPAPI,
COM automation and registry writes can resemble a loader or stealer. Here the
actual data flows implement the advertised application. No attacker endpoint,
preloaded hostile invite, credential collection or hidden task dispatcher was
found. Historical publisher trust and actual deployment authorization remain
unknown. One native x86 byte-pattern hit was inside GZip resource bytes at
0xfcd2, not a decoded native instruction.

1e20bc257f7c637a95f935d613d9a9c17eede935f3ed96c1edd8c96c1cf6403e
Identification: XMRig 6.26.0 static Linux x86-64 miner, renamed systemd-ntpd.
Verdict: BENIGN artifact; no modified mining code or abusive configuration.

The first 8,350,992 bytes are identical to the official static release's xmrig
binary (SHA256 b20f39fc00d242e706b6c30367ad811c676e0575050a4ec2f30104b696944b49).
The supplied file adds 64 opaque bytes after the original ELF section table.
The ELF entry, segments, initializers and code are unchanged, so those bytes
are not an added mapped payload. No code referencing an appended configuration
or a wallet/pool override was found. This does not assign a purpose to the tail.
Official archive SHA256:
fc6f8ae5f64e4f17481f7e3be29a1c56949f216a998414188003eae1db20c9e5
https://github.com/xmrig/xmrig/releases/download/v6.26.0/xmrig-6.26.0-linux-static-x64.tar.gz
https://xmrig.com/download

Rizin follows ELF entry 0x40e5f3 to libc startup and main at 0x40d280, constructing
Process, handling CLI Entry operations, then App construction/execution.
Compared this exact-code identity with upstream v6.26.0 App.cpp, Process.cpp,
Entry.cpp, Config_default.h, BasicCpuInfo.cpp and RxMsr.cpp. App::exec checks
controller readiness, handles background/dry-run options, initializes mining,
and enters libuv. It obtains configured work via Stratum and submits hashes.
Hugepage allocation, CPU/DMI inventory and MSR tuning are mining performance
features; they do not by themselves demonstrate VM evasion or escalation.
The executable has standard donation/benchmark endpoints and normal external
configuration support; no attacker-specific pool or wallet was recovered.
https://github.com/xmrig/xmrig/tree/v6.26.0/src

Why collected/flagged: XMRig is often deployed for cryptojacking, and the supplied
systemd-like filename plus unexplained trailer warrant deployment investigation.
The provided Triage report actually identifies XMRig and CPU/hardware inventory;
its high score does not establish Mirai, exploitation, brute force or propagation.
https://tria.ge/261017-m7hzxastdy
Without the installing script/service, live command line, config.json, owner
consent, pool ownership or host timeline, unauthorized mining cannot be
established from this stock executable. Retain all accurate mining and system
capability traits regardless of verdict.

Trait changes and focused controls

Relocated the two Office executable-name atoms and their name-set composite
from objectives/command-and-control/dropper/sideload to the existing
micro-behaviors/fs/path/basename leaf. These are bare basenames in content,
not scanned filenames, executable-path evidence, execution or sideloading.
The name-set composite is notable with no ATT&CK claim. It also applies to
signed artifacts: a signature does not erase a name reference.
Relocated the exact and loose mavinject32 name atoms out of metadata layout
ratios to the same basename leaf, promoting their complete references from
component to notable. Preserved their matchers and scopes; updated every exact
consumer in oracle-onenote, signed-nsis-bundle and Elex. All other rules in the
source files remain unchanged. Ancestor selectors were checked; broad layout
selectors lose only nonstructural names, filesystem selectors gain accurately
placed path references. Target sample rescans show no unintended convictions.
No filename/hash/sample-specific exception was introduced.

Excluded IL-only CLR images from x86-imul-31 using the parsed
pe.clr.is_il_only metric. Native PE, ELF and Mach-O opcode coverage remains.
No YAML change was necessary to XMRig capabilities or Atom's product identity.
The six generated PE controls in check.py verify both name pairs, a single
name, extension near misses, native IMUL preservation and managed-data exclusion.
They all pass. Initial and final atomscan plus cleave facts were run for every
sample. Final local full reports show zero hostile and zero suspicious findings
for each sample, including all 13 analysis units of the DismHost concatenation.
Raw facts' speculative XOR/Base64/hex decoded candidates were reviewed as leads;
several are transforms of ordinary import strings, not actual obfuscation.
